claim: Neurons in the mouse superior colliculus (SC) encode visual saliency by detecting motion contrast between stimulus center and surround.
source: Here, we show that neurons in the mouse superior colliculus (SC) encode visual saliency by detecting motion contrast between stimulus center and surround.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript including calcium imaging experiments showing differential responses to center-surround motion contrast.

claim: Excitatory neurons in the most superficial lamina of the SC are contextually modulated, monotonically increasing their response from suppression by the same-direction surround to maximal potentiation by an oppositely-moving surround.
source: Excitatory neurons in the most superficial lamina of the SC are contextually modulated, monotonically increasing their response from suppression by the same-direction surround to maximal potentiation by an oppositely-moving surround.
evidence: Supported by data in Figures 1 and 2 showing response modulation patterns of excitatory neurons to different center-surround direction combinations.

claim: The degree of potentiation by opposite-direction surround declines with depth in the SC.
source: The degree of this potentiation declines with depth in the SC.
evidence: Supported by depth-dependent imaging data shown in Figure 6C demonstrating that potentiation gradually turns into suppression with increasing depth.

claim: Inhibitory neurons are suppressed by any surround at all depths.
source: Inhibitory neurons are suppressed by any surround at all depths.
evidence: Supported by data in Figures 3 and 6F-G showing suppression of inhibitory neurons by both same and opposite direction surrounds across different depths.

claim: Response modulations in both excitatory and inhibitory neuronal populations are much more prominent to direction contrast than to phase, temporal frequency, or static orientation contrast.
source: These response modulations in both neuronal populations are much more prominent to direction contrast than to phase, temporal frequency, or static orientation contrast, suggesting feature-specific saliency encoding in the mouse SC.
evidence: Supported by comparative data in Figure 5 showing differential modulation indices for direction contrast versus other types of feature contrast.

claim: V1 neurons are suppressed by stimuli of the same orientation in regions surrounding the RF.
source: It was shown that V1 neurons are suppressed by stimuli of the same orientation in regions surrounding the RF (Jones et al., 2002; Knierim and van Essen, 1992; Sengpiel et al., 1997), consistent with the classical surround suppression seen at the level of the retina and lateral geniculate nucleus (Sachdev et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies in primate and cat V1.

claim: V1 neurons displayed lower levels of suppression when static gratings of orthogonal orientations were shown in the surround.
source: Importantly, V1 neurons displayed lower levels of suppression when static gratings of orthogonal orientations were shown in the surround (Kastner et al., 1999; Knierim and van Essen, 1992; Nothdurft et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Orthogonal surrounds were able to induce response facilitation in primate V1 in response to moving gratings.
source: In response to moving gratings, orthogonal surrounds were even able to induce a certain level of response facilitation in primate V1 (Jones et al., 2001; Jones et al., 2002; Sillito et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies in primate V1.

claim: The superior colliculus contains a saliency map.
source: Although the exact location of where the saliency map is first generated is still a matter of debate, there is a general agreement that the superior colliculus (SC) in the midbrain contains such a map (Veale et al., 2017; Zhaoping, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work on saliency maps.

claim: In primates, SC neurons are not tuned to specific visual properties.
source: In primates, SC neurons are not tuned to specific visual properties, consistent with the notion of feature-agnostic saliency representation (White et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study on primate SC.

claim: In lower vertebrates such as fish and birds, neurons in the optic tectum can perform feature-specific saliency computations.
source: In contrast, in lower vertebrates such as fish and birds, where neocortex has not evolved, neurons in the optic tectum, the homologue of the mammalian SC, can perform certain feature-specific saliency computations (Ben-Tov et al., 2015; Frost et al., 1981; Sun et al., 2002; Zahar et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies in fish and birds.

claim: Most visual neurons in the mouse SC are tuned to features such as motion direction or stimulus orientation.
source: Unlike in primates, most visual neurons in the mouse SC are tuned to features such as motion direction or stimulus orientation (Gale and Murphy, 2014; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on mouse SC.

claim: The SC is the most prominent retinal target in mice and mediates visually-guided behaviors.
source: Although neurons in mouse V1 show similar selectivity compared to those in higher mammals (Niell and Stryker, 2008), the SC remains the most prominent retinal target in mice, and mediates visually-guided behaviors (Ellis et al., 2016; Liang et al., 2015; Shang et al., 2015; Wei et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on mouse SC function.

claim: About half of sSGS neurons were responsive to drifting gratings.
source: Consistent with our previous finding, about half of sSGS neurons were responsive to the drifting gratings (n = 355/811 GAD2- and n = 379/652 GAD2+, from 9 mice, see Materials and methods for details of determining responsiveness)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the imaging experiments reported in the manuscript.

claim: Most responsive sSGS neurons were direction selective (73.0% of GAD2- and 63.1% of GAD2+ neurons had gDSI ≥0.25).
source: and most of them were direction selective (DS), showing much higher increases in fluorescence to their preferred direction than to the opposite direction (Figure 1C; 259/355, 73.0% of GAD2-, and 239/379, 63.1% of GAD2+ neurons had gDSI ≥0.25).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the imaging experiments with specific percentages and cell counts.

claim: For most responsive excitatory neurons (82.8%), the small patch of gratings covered their entire RFs.
source: For most responsive excitatory neurons (n = 294/355, 82.8%), the small patch of gratings covered their entire RFs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from receptive field mapping experiments.

claim: When both center and surround gratings moved along the preferred direction, classical surround-suppression of the center response was observed in excitatory neurons.
source: In the case when both the center and surround gratings moved along the preferred direction of a given excitatory neuron, we saw a classical surround-suppression of the center response (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C-D demonstrating reduced responses when same-direction surround is added.

claim: When the preferred direction in the center was coupled with a surround stimulus of opposite direction, most excitatory sSGS neurons increased their responses.
source: In striking contrast, when the preferred direction in the center was coupled with a surround stimulus of opposite direction, most excitatory sSGS neurons increased their responses (Figure 1C,E).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1C and 1E showing potentiation of responses with opposite-direction surround.

claim: Excitatory sSGS neurons are bidirectionally modulated depending on what is shown in the surround.
source: In other words, to the same stimulus in their RF center, excitatory sSGS neurons could increase or decrease their response, that is, they are bidirectionally modulated, depending on what is shown in the surround.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing both suppression and potentiation depending on surround direction.

claim: A substantial population of excitatory sSGS neurons (23.6%) did not respond to center or surround gratings when presented separately but became responsive to particular Center-Surround combinations.
source: Interestingly, a substantial population of excitatory sSGS neurons did not respond to the center or the surround gratings when presented separately but became responsive to particular Center-Surround (C-S) combinations (n = 191/811, 23.6%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the imaging experiments identifying a specific population of 'center-silent' neurons.

claim: The majority of center-silent neurons (80.6%) had mappable RFs that were covered by the center patch.
source: This was despite the fact that the majority of these cells (154/191, 80.6%) had mappable RFs that were covered by the center patch (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from receptive field mapping of center-silent neurons.

claim: Over the entire population of excitatory sSGS cells, the response to the preferred center stimulus became smaller with the introduction of the same direction surround in 83.3% of cells.
source: Over the entire population of these excitatory sSGS cells (n = 355 "center responsive" + 191 "center silent" = 546), the response to the "preferred center" stimulus became smaller with the introduction of the same direction surround in 83.3% of cells (n = 455/546)
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the modulation data across the population.

claim: The response became larger in 74.7% of excitatory cells when the surround was moving in the opposite direction.
source: and larger in 74.7% of cells (n = 408/546) when the surround was moving in the opposite direction (Fig. 1G, Kolmogorov Smirnov [KS] test, p = 4.0e-83, KS stat = 0.59).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary with statistical testing showing significant potentiation by opposite surround.

claim: The modulation of center responses by surround was geometric in nature, ranging from divisive suppression by the same surround to multiplicative potentiation by the opposite surround.
source: Interestingly, this modulation was geometric in nature, ranging from a divisive suppression by the same surround to a multiplicative potentiation by the opposite surround (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the linear relationship analysis shown in Figure 2C with specific slopes indicating divisive and multiplicative effects.

claim: A linear modulation of the center responses was seen with intermediate differences between C-S directions.
source: In fact, a linear modulation of the center responses was also seen with intermediate differences between C-S directions (e.g., Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2D showing linear relationships for orthogonal-direction surrounds.

claim: The slope of linear relationships between center and center-surround responses gradually increased with the C-S direction difference.
source: We thus calculated the slope of these linear relationships (i.e., fold changes of center responses by the surround), and found that it gradually increased with the C-S direction difference (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2E demonstrating monotonic tuning to motion contrast.

claim: Excitatory sSGS neurons were monotonically tuned to motion contrast, showing maximal responses to the most salient stimulus with oppositely-moving center and surround.
source: In other words, excitatory sSGS neurons were monotonically tuned to motion contrast, showing maximal responses to the most salient stimulus with oppositely-moving center and surround.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the data showing increasing slope with C-S direction difference.

claim: Center-silent neurons showed an emergent, monotonically increasing response as the C-S direction difference increased.
source: Finally, we performed a similar analysis for the 'center silent' neurons (n = 191), by averaging their responses to particular C-S direction differences. An emergent, and again monotonically increasing, response was seen as the C-S direction difference increased (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2F showing increasing responses with increasing C-S direction difference.

claim: Inhibitory sSGS neurons experienced surround suppression when the surround direction matched the direction in the RF center.
source: Just like excitatory neurons, inhibitory neurons also experienced surround suppression when the surround direction matched the direction in the RF center (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3A-B showing reduced responses with same-direction surround.

claim: Inhibitory neurons were significantly less suppressed by same-direction surround than excitatory neurons.
source: They were, however, significantly less suppressed than their excitatory counterparts (Figure 4A, KS test, p=6.0e-20, KS stat = 0.30).
evidence: This is a comparative statistical analysis between GAD2+ and GAD2- neurons shown in Figure 4A.

claim: When the surround grating drifted in the opposite direction, inhibitory neurons' response to the preferred center stimulus was strongly suppressed.
source: Furthermore, when the surround grating drifted in the opposite direction, the inhibitory neurons' response to the preferred center stimulus was quite strongly suppressed (Figure 3A and C).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3A and 3C showing suppression rather than potentiation in inhibitory neurons.

claim: The response of inhibitory neurons to opposite-direction surround is in stark contrast with the potentiation seen in excitatory sSGS neurons.
source: This is in stark contrast with the potentiation seen in excitatory sSGS neurons under the same conditions (Figure 4B, KS test, p=1.46e-58, KS stat = 0.51).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Fewer center-silent inhibitory cells became responsive when opposite center and surround was shown compared to excitatory neurons, and their responses were weaker.
source: Consistently, compared with excitatory neurons, fewer 'center-silent' inhibitory cells became responsive when opposite center and surround was shown and their responses were weaker (n = 85/652; Figure 3D, compare with Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a comparative quantitative observation between GAD2+ and GAD2- center-silent neurons.

claim: The suppression by the opposite surround was greater than that by the same-direction surround for most inhibitory neurons.
source: Overall, the suppression by the opposite surround was even greater than that by the same-direction surround for most inhibitory neurons (Figure 3E, KS test, p=3.2e-6, KS stat = 0.17)
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of modulation indices shown in Figure 3E.

claim: A much larger proportion of excitatory sSGS neurons (50.2%) was significantly potentiated by the opposite-direction surround compared to inhibitory neurons (9.9%).
source: Consistently, using this method, we found that a much larger proportion of excitatory sSGS neurons was significantly potentiated by the opposite-direction surround (n = 274 out of 546 responsive cells, 50.2%), compared to inhibitory neurons (n = 46 out of 464, 9.9%; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison using bootstrapping analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Many center-responsive inhibitory neurons (53.8%) could be activated by a surround alone that was moving in their preferred direction.
source: Finally, we found that many center-responsive inhibitory neurons (204/379, 53.8%) could be activated by a surround alone that was moving in their preferred direction (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, blue curve).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the imaging data showing responses to surround-alone stimuli.

claim: Response to surround alone was rarely observed in excitatory neurons.
source: Such a response profile was rarely observed in excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is a comparative observation between GAD2+ and GAD2- neurons.

claim: Excitatory and inhibitory neurons had similar RF sizes when mapped with flashing squares.
source: This was quite surprising given the fact that excitatory and inhibitory neurons had similar RF sizes when mapped with flashing squares (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–F, p=0.19, Mann-Whitney U-test comparing their RF size in panels E-F, n = 542 GAD2- and 425 GAD2+ neurons responsive to flashing squares).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison with statistical testing of receptive field sizes.

claim: The 2-dimensional standard deviation of GAD2+ RF centroids for any given imaging field of view was statistically larger than that of GAD2- ones.
source: This was true to some extent. The 2-dimensional standard deviation of GAD2+ RF centroids for any given imaging field of view was statistically larger than that of GAD2- ones (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G and H, p=0.03, paired t-test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from analysis of RF centroid distributions shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2G-H.

claim: The anti-phase surround resulted in an attenuated suppression (or even a slight potentiation) in both GAD2- and GAD2+ neurons compared to the in-phase surround.
source: Compared to the in-phase surround ('Same S'), which strongly suppressed sSGS responses to the center stimulus, the anti-phase surround resulted in an attenuated suppression (or even a slight potentiation) in both GAD2- and GAD2+ neurons (Figure 5B–C; compare the green and the red dashed lines in Figure 5B, p=2.2e-10, and Figure 5C, p=6.2e-6).
evidence: This is supported by comparative data with statistical testing shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: Either lower (1 Hz) or higher (4 Hz) temporal frequencies in the surround elicited a similar attenuation of response suppression compared to a uniform (2 Hz) temporal frequency between center and surround.
source: Similar responses were seen when we varied the temporal frequency of the surround grating. Either lower (1 Hz, red dotted) or higher (4 Hz, navy blue dotted) temporal frequencies in the surround elicited a similar attenuation of response suppression compared to a uniform (2 Hz, solid green) temporal frequency between center and surround (compare the solid green line to the dotted red and blue lines in Figure 5B–C, p<0.01 for both comparisons).
evidence: This is supported by comparative data with statistical testing shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: The attenuated suppression seen with anti-phase, lower and higher temporal frequency surrounds did not reach the level of potentiation experienced by excitatory neurons to an oppositely-moving surround.
source: Importantly, the attenuated suppression seen in these 3 sets of center-surround contrast (anti-phase, and lower and higher temporal frequency) did not reach the level of potentiation experienced by the same excitatory neurons to an oppositely-moving surround (solid red line in Figure 5B, n = 73, 3 mice, KS test, p<0.01 for all comparisons).
evidence: This is a comparative statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The heightened level of suppression experienced by inhibitory neurons to an oppositely-moving surround could not be matched by anti-phase or temporal frequency contrast conditions.
source: In the same vein, the heightened level of suppression experienced by inhibitory neurons to an oppositely-moving surround could not be matched either under the aforementioned conditions (solid red line in Figure 5C, n = 124, 3 mice, KS test, p<0.01 for all comparisons).
evidence: This is a comparative statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Both GAD2- and GAD2+ neurons experienced a slightly attenuated level of suppression under cross-surround conditions compared to iso-surround for static gratings, but no potentiation.
source: Next, we tested static gratings with varying orientations. Consistent with their selectivity for the direction of moving stimuli, sSGS neurons showed weaker responses to static gratings (data not shown). More relevant to the current study, both GAD2- and GAD2+ neurons experienced a slightly attenuated level of suppression under cross-surround conditions, but no potentiation, compared to iso-surround (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5D-E showing modulation indices for static orientation contrast.

claim: Excitatory neurons appeared to be more strongly suppressed than inhibitory neurons by static gratings regardless of the surround orientation.
source: In addition, the excitatory neurons (i.e., GAD2-) appeared to be more strongly suppressed than the inhibitory neurons (i.e., GAD2+) regardless of the surround orientation (Compare same-colored distributions in Figure 5D and E; Iso-surround GAD2- vs. GAD2+, KS test, p=1.6e-8, KS stat = 0.37; Cross-surround GAD2- vs. GAD2+, KS test, p=9.7e-7, KS stat = 0.33).
evidence: This is a comparative statistical analysis between GAD2- and GAD2+ neurons for static orientation stimuli.

claim: The bidirectional modulation of activity observed in GAD2- vs. GAD2+ neurons under C-S motion direction contrast was not observed under static orientation opponency conditions.
source: In other words, the bidirectional modulation of activity that we observed in GAD2- vs. GAD2+ neurons under C-S motion direction contrast was not observed under static orientation opponency conditions.
evidence: This is an interpretive summary of the comparative data between motion and static orientation conditions.

claim: sSGS neurons show specificity of saliency responses to motion direction contrast between the center and surround.
source: Altogether, these observations reveal a specificity of saliency responses in sSGS neurons to motion direction contrast between the center and surround.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the feature contrast comparison experiments.

claim: Direction selectivity in the mouse SGS declines with depth.
source: Studies in a number of species have shown that the visual layers of the SC or optic tectum can be further divided into sub-laminae (May, 2006). Indeed, based on a small number of single unit recordings, we recently found that direction selectivity in the mouse SGS declines with depth (Inayat et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and confirmed by data in the current study.

claim: The decline in direction selectivity with depth was observed for both excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
source: Importantly, our results indicate that the decline was observed for both excitatory (Figure 6B, KS test, p=1.7e-16, KS stat = 0.62, between the most superficial (black) and deepest (magenta) cell populations) and inhibitory neurons (Figure 6E, KS test, p=4.6e-7, KS stat = 0.39).
evidence: This is supported by depth-dependent imaging data with statistical testing shown in Figure 6B and 6E.

claim: Response potentiation of excitatory neurons by oppositely-moving surround gradually turned into suppression with depth.
source: Interestingly, this potentiation gradually turned into suppression with depth (Figure 6C, KS test, p<0.01 between the four depths).
evidence: This is supported by depth-dependent analysis shown in Figure 6C with statistical testing.

claim: Surround of the same direction remained suppressive across depth in excitatory neurons, despite some subtle difference.
source: On the other hand, surround of the same direction remained suppressive across depth, despite some subtle difference (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by depth-dependent analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: No significant change was seen in the opposite surround modulation index with depth for inhibitory neurons.
source: In the case of inhibitory neurons, no significant change was seen in the opposite surround modulation index with depth (Figure 6F)
evidence: This is supported by depth-dependent analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: A significant correlation was seen between modulation index and gDSI for excitatory neurons (r = 0.38, p=1.3e-14).
source: Indeed, a significant, albeit noisy, correlation was seen between the two variables for excitatory neurons (Figure 7A, r = 0.38, p=1.3e-14), where highly DS neurons tend to be potentiated by the opposite surround, while the non-selective ones tend to be suppressed.
evidence: This is a statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: A negative correlation was observed for inhibitory neurons between the modulation index and gDSI (r = −0.42, p=4.2e-24).
source: In contrast, we observed a negative correlation for inhibitory neurons between the modulation index and gDSI (Figure 7B, r = −0.42, p=4.2e-24), where the highly DS cells were much more suppressed by the opposite surround.
evidence: This is a statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: A positive correlation was seen between the modulation index and gDSI for inhibitory neurons when the same surround was presented (r = 0.43, p=8.1e-26).
source: Interestingly, a positive correlation was seen between the modulation index and gDSI for inhibitory neurons when the same surround was presented (Figure 7C, r = 0.43, p=8.1e-26).
evidence: This is a statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Inhibitory neurons appear to form two clusters based on their gDSI.
source: Imaging deeper into the SGS also allowed us to reveal an intriguing property of inhibitory neurons. These cells appear to form two clusters based on their gDSI (Figure 7B–C).
evidence: This is an observation from the scatter plots in Figure 7B-C showing distinct populations.

claim: More direction-selective inhibitory cells (gDSI ≥ 0.5) were much more susceptible to suppression by the opposite direction surround compared to less selective counterparts.
source: The more DS cells (gDSI ≥ 0.5) were much more susceptible to suppression by the opposite direction surround compared to less selective counterparts (Figure 7B, KS test, p=1.1e-19, KS stat = 0.41, between the 'gDSI ≥ 0.5' and 'gDSI < 0.5' populations; Figure 7D, Mann-Whitney U-test, p=3.7e-19, between 'gDSI ≥0.5 Opp.' and 'gDSI < 0.5 Opp.")
evidence: This is a comparative statistical analysis between high and low gDSI inhibitory neurons shown in Figure 7B and 7D.

claim: More direction-selective inhibitory cells were much less susceptible to suppression by the same surround.
source: and much less susceptible to suppression by the same surround (Figure 7C, KS test, p=2.5e-19, KS stat = 0.40, between the 'gDSI ≥ 0.5' and 'gDSI < 0.5' populations; Figure 7D, Mann-Whitney U-test, p=7.5e-24, between 'gDSI ≥ 0.5 Same' and 'gDSI < 0.5 Same').
evidence: This is a comparative statistical analysis between high and low gDSI inhibitory neurons shown in Figure 7C and 7D.

claim: Visual cortex was removed to allow optical access and eliminate any potential cortical influence on SC responses.
source: Visual cortex was removed to allow optical access and eliminate any potential cortical influence on SC responses (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the experimental procedure.

claim: The superficial SGS is enriched with neurons that are highly selective for movement direction.
source: We specifically imaged the most superficial lamina of the SGS (sSGS,<50 μm from the surface), which we have recently shown to be enriched with neurons that are highly selective for movement direction (Inayat et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The greater suppression of inhibitory neurons by the opposite-direction surround suggests a possible role for them in mediating the potentiation of excitatory neurons through disinhibition.
source: The greater suppression of inhibitory neurons by the opposite-direction surround suggests a possible role for them in mediating the potentiation of excitatory neurons through disinhibition.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the differential responses observed in excitatory and inhibitory neurons.

claim: Visual cortex may limit context-dependent modulation by cross-oriented gratings in the SGS.
source: This is consistent with the findings of a recent electrophysiological study suggesting that visual cortex may actually limit context-dependent modulation by cross-oriented gratings in the SGS (Ahmadlou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Contextual modulation was more prominent in awake mice than in anesthetized mice.
source: The same study also showed that this type of contextual modulation was more prominent in awake mice than in anesthetized mice (Ahmadlou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Retinal inputs were shown to be the source of direction selectivity in the SGS.
source: Retinal inputs, on the other hand, were shown to be the source of direction selectivity in the SGS (Shi et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Surround-modulated suppression was observed under several motion-contrast regimes in direction-selective retinal ganglion cells in rabbits.
source: Surround-modulated suppression was observed under several motion-contrast regimes (spatial phase, spatial frequency, and velocity) in direction-selective retinal ganglion cells (DSGCs) in rabbits (Chiao and Masland, 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study in rabbit retina.

claim: Orientation-specific surround modulation of RGCs was shown in rats.
source: and orientation-specific surround modulation of RGCs was shown in rats (Girman and Lund, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study in rat retina.

claim: Object motion sensitive (OMS) RGCs were found in rabbits and salamander, which are suppressed by global motion but respond strongly to motion difference between RF center and surround.
source: Furthermore, object motion sensitive ('OMS') RGCs were found in rabbits and salamander, which are suppressed by global motion but respond strongly to motion difference between RF center and surround (Olveczky et al., 2003; Baccus et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies in rabbit and salamander retina.

claim: The OMS cells included several RGC types, and their selectivity for differential motion is independent of direction.
source: The OMS cells included several RGC types, and their selectivity for differential motion is independent of direction (Olveczky et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study on OMS cells.

claim: In mouse DSGCs, the oppositely-moving surround elicits smaller suppression than the same-direction surround, but never reaches potentiation.
source: They showed that the oppositely-moving surround elicits smaller suppression than the same-direction surround, but never reaches potentiation; and the anti-phase surround causes similar responses as the opposite surround.
evidence: This claim is based on unpublished personal communication from other researchers.

claim: Some of the SC responses, including the suppression by same surround and its attenuation by anti-phase and cross-oriented static gratings, are likely inherited from the retina.
source: These retinal studies thus suggest that some of the SC responses, including the suppression by same surround and its attenuation by anti-phase and cross-oriented static gratings, are likely inherited from the retina.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with retinal studies cited in the discussion.

claim: The bidirectional encoding of motion direction contrast by sSGS neurons is not inherited from the retina.
source: However, these and other observations indicate that the bidirectional encoding of motion direction contrast by sSGS neurons is not inherited from the retina.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with retinal studies and differences observed in SC responses.

claim: The modulation by out-of-phase and opposite surround is nearly identical in DSGCs, but dramatically different in the sSGS.
source: Most notably, the modulation by out-of-phase and opposite surround is nearly identical in DSGCs, but dramatically different in the sSGS.
evidence: This is a comparative observation between retinal and SC responses supporting the claim that SC responses are not simply inherited from retina.

claim: The fact that excitatory and inhibitory neurons in the sSGS exhibit strikingly different responses to center-surround stimuli argues for a role of intracollicular circuit mechanisms.
source: Additionally, the fact that excitatory and inhibitory neurons in the sSGS, both of which receive direct retinal input (Shi et al., 2017), exhibit strikingly different responses to center-surround stimuli argues for a role of intracollicular circuit mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential responses observed in excitatory and inhibitory neurons that both receive retinal input.

claim: Intracollicular circuits may include long range excitatory and inhibitory connections from the surround, wired in a direction- and cell-type-specific manner.
source: These circuits may include long range excitatory and inhibitory connections from the surround, and they must be wired in a direction- and cell-type-specific manner to mediate the differential responses in excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic proposal based on the observed response properties.

claim: The circuits mediating direction contrast responses are likely restricted to the superficial SGS to account for the depth-specific changes.
source: They are also likely restricted to the superficial SGS to account for the depth-specific changes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the depth-dependent changes in response properties observed in the study.

claim: The transformation from feature-specific saliency analysis to a feature-agnostic saliency map may take place between the deep SGS and the intermediate layers of the SC.
source: It is therefore possible that the transformation from a feature-specific saliency analysis to a feature-agnostic saliency map, or even more generally to a modality-agnostic saliency map, takes place between the deep SGS and the intermediate layers of the SC.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the depth-dependent changes and known properties of SC layers.

claim: The comparison of SC response properties across vertebrate species supports the idea of a gradual evolutionary migration of saliency computation from a single locus in the SC/OT to a multi-structural process that involves cortical inputs.
source: Importantly, the comparison of SC response properties across vertebrate species, including our current findings, supports the idea of a gradual evolutionary migration of saliency computation from a single locus in the SC/OT to a multi-structural process that involves cortical inputs (Zhaoping, 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretive claim connecting the current findings to evolutionary theory, supported by citation.

claim: The inhibitory circuits in the rodent SGS have only been studied in the context of classical surround suppression, mostly using stimulus size tuning as a measure of modulation.
source: The inhibitory circuits in the rodent SGS have only been studied in the context of classical surround suppression, mostly using stimulus size tuning as a measure of modulation (Binns and Salt, 1997; Kasai and Isa, 2016).
evidence: This is a summary of previous literature supported by citations.

claim: A recent two-photon imaging study in the mouse SGS showed that the activity of local inhibitory and excitatory neurons is equally suppressed by the surround, implicating long range inhibitory input in mediating the phenomenon.
source: A recent two-photon imaging study in the mouse SGS showed that the activity of local inhibitory and excitatory neurons is equally suppressed by the surround, implicating long range inhibitory input in mediating the phenomenon (Kasai and Isa, 2016).

claim: Adult C57BL/6 mice of both sexes were used in this study (n = 24, 2–4 months old).
